extracted.intended_audience: scientists, naturalists, and educated public interested in paleontology and geology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological principles for interpreting fossils, reconstructing extinct organisms, correlating strata, and inferring past environments and biological change from the fossil record. Emphasizes empirical rules (e.g., like effects imply like causes), biostratigraphy, and limits of inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental problem of paleontology
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a body endowed with a certain shape and produced in accordance with natural laws, to find in that body itself the evidence of the place and manner of its production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated by Steno (De Solido intra Solidum). The investigator must look for internal evidence in a fossil and its matrix to determine how and where it was produced. This defines the primary investigative aim of paleontology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom: like effects imply like causes
rubrics_metrics.description: "Bodies which are altogether similar have been produced in the same way." (Steno's formulation of the axiom 'like effects imply like causes'.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the basic methodological principle throughout paleontological inference: morphological similarity implies similar biological origin or cause. This axiom underlies reconstruction, identification, and environmental interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction from parts (inference from part to whole)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconstructing an extinct animal from a tooth or a bone by applying empirical knowledge of the coordination of parts in living animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only possible when the recovered part presents peculiarities known by prior experience to be characteristic of a certain group. Examples: glossopetrae identified as shark teeth by dissecting a shark; cow's grinder and horse's grinder allowing inference about foot structure and digestion. Warning: not every tooth or bone suffices — reconstructions require characteristic, diagnostic features and broad comparative experience; misreconstruction is an anti-pattern when based on insufficient or non-characteristic parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fossils as environmental indicators (marine vs terrestrial vs freshwater)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fossils resembling terrestrial or freshwater organisms are evidence of land or fresh water; fossils resembling marine organisms are evidence of the sea at the time they were living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the absence of contrary evidence, infer that the environment indicated by the organism existed at the locality when the organism was alive. This is the basis for using fossils to decipher the history of the earth (e.g., Steno, Buffon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biostratigraphy / principle of faunal succession (William Smith)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each stratum contains certain fossils which are peculiar to it; and the order in which the strata characterized by these fossils are superimposed one upon the other is always the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the fossil content to identify and correlate strata of the same relative age across discontinuities or compositional changes. This enables relative dating and global correlation of sedimentary layers; it is one of the best-established empirical truths in geology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fossils as evidence for temporal depth of life (inference of vast time)
rubrics_metrics.description: If fossils are organic remains and stratified rocks are sedimentary deposits, then living matter has existed upon the earth for a vast length of time (millions of years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine biostratigraphy and sedimentary interpretation to infer duration of past time. This conclusion depends on accepting the two foundational propositions (fossils = remains; stratification = sedimentary deposition). If those assumptions fail, the temporal inference collapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of succession of forms and inference of gradual modification
rubrics_metrics.description: The succession of species in time shows continual changes: in many groups, a series of successive forms presents gradual modification consistent with production by gradual modification of earlier forms (evolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare series of forms through time (stage-by-stage) within a type (e.g., horse series, ungulates, carnivora) to assess trends such as increasing specialization. Recent paleontological discoveries are judged to be in accordance with the hypothesis of evolution; alternative hypotheses (innumerable independent creations or spontaneous generation) are considered less probable. Use broad, well-sampled stratigraphic series for such inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fossil assemblages to infer past climates, extinctions, and geographic change
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns in fossil occurrence (e.g., marine shells inland, fossils of species not now present in nearby seas, northern occurrences of elephant/hippopotamus remains, widespread tusks) indicate past sea coverage, different climatic conditions (warmer polar regions), extinctions, and shifts in distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buffon's five classes of fossil monuments illustrate how different types of fossil evidence support specific inferences about past environments, climate change, extinction events, and the role of geological change in species distribution. Multiple lines of fossil evidence strengthen such reconstructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative serial study requirement for determining relations among successive species
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the relation of successive species one must compare, stage by stage, the series of forms presented by one and the same type throughout a long span of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed, contiguous stratigraphic series (long uninterrupted records) are necessary to demonstrate gradual specialization or transitional forms. Partial or poorly sampled series are insufficient to settle relations reliably; the horse series is cited as a successful example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational conditions and limits of paleontological inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Paleontology rests upon two propositions: (1) fossils are remains of animals and plants; and (2) the stratified rocks in which they are found are sedimentary deposits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If either proposition is false (e.g., fossils are mere mineral 'figured stones' or stratification results from processes unlike modern sedimentation), paleontology lacks a foundation and its inferences (relative ages, environmental reconstructions, and evolutionary conclusions) are invalid. Historical anti-patterns include spontaneous-generation explanations and 'plastic force' interpretations of fossils when fossilization chemistry was not understood.
